newsitem.title: INDIA: India seen cutting deposit rates to lower lending rates.
newsitem.headline: India seen cutting deposit rates to lower lending rates.

text.p: Bankers said on Wednesday they expected the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to announce a cut in deposit interest rates to enable banks to reduce lending rates and boost sagging industrial production.
The RBI issues its half-yearly credit policy statement on April 15, which will chart a strategy that fits in with Finance Minister P.Chidambaram's pro-growth and investment budget.

"The lowering of the interest rate cap seems a distinct possibility given the stated intentions of both the central bank and the government to bring down interest rates," M.S. Verma, State Bank of India (SBI) chairman told Reuters.
SBI is India's largest commercial bank.
Current RBI rules allow banks to offer a maximum of 10 percent per annum for deposits with maturities up to one year.
Bankers said they expected this to be reduced to at least nine percent.
"If banks are to lower lending rates their cost of funds also has to come down," Verma said.
Industrialists have complained that Indian interest rates are too high, threatening viability of projects and forcing them to defer investment decisions until rates fall.
High interest rates in 1995/96, when banks charged best borrowers as much as 18-19 percent, forced industry to defer investment decisions, leading to a slowdown in the current year, analysts say.

Chidambaram's budget proposals revived optimism, but the withdrawal of Congress party support for Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's minority government has left the coalition fighting for survival with the budget still unpassed by parliament.
India's industrial production grew 8.3 percent year-on-year in April-December 1996 against 11.4 percent the previous year, the government said on Monday.

"Long-term interest rates are around 19 to 20 percent and inflation is around 7.0 percent -- the difference is too wide," said Yeshwant Deosthalee, vice-president and director at engineering and constructon firm Larsen & Toubro Ltd.
"On short-term funds, the difference is narrowing. Eventually it has to fall to around 4.0 percent. This won't happen unless deposit rates are cut," Deosthalee said.

Banks cut prime lending rates by 100 to 150 basis points during 1996/97 (April-March) after the RBI took steps to boost liquidity with the banking system, responding to industry's complaints of a funds crunch and high interest.

Between April 1996 and January 1997, the central bank cut banks' cash reserve ratios (CRR) by four percentage points. Most banks responded by reducing prime lending rates by one to one and half percentage points.
Leading state-run banks charge between 14.0-14.5 percent to their prime borrowers.
"I think that enough has been done on the liquidity front," said Paresh Sukthankar, vice-president at the private HDFC Bank.
"I don't see the need for any further cut in CRR at the moment," he said. "But a cut in deposit rates will enable banks to lower their cost of funds and reduce lending rates."

"Basically what this will do is to convey is a strong signal to financial markets that interest rates are headed south," Sukthankar said. "I think at the moment, industry is still sceptical whether rates will remain low over a period of time."
Not everyone is convinced interest rates will fall.
"Lending rates have bottomed out. I don't see PLR falling below 14 percent," said Aditya Samant, economist at UBS Securities at Hong Kong.
He said he did not see inflation, currently 7.5 percent measured by the wholesale price index, coming down over the next 12 to 18 months. --Bombay Newsroom, (91) 22-265 9000
